summaries.example: Imagine a class sorting animals. “Animal” can describe many individual creatures, such as one dog or one cat. Alberic thought that this shared kind was more than just a word. He treated it as something real in the things themselves, even though it is understood by the mind as a general idea.
summaries.summary: Alberic of Paris was a leading teacher in twelfth-century Paris, when the city was becoming an important center of learning. Very little is known about his personal life, and none of his writings are known to survive. We learn about his ideas from later texts, especially works connected with his students and followers. Alberic became famous for opposing Peter Abelard and the Nominalists, a school that placed strong emphasis on words and names. Alberic believed that logic had to deal with things in the world, not only with language. In his metaphysics, he defended real universals: kinds such as animal and human are not merely names, though they do not exist separately from individual animals and humans. He also discussed predication, or what can truly be said of one thing about another, and argued that time is a special kind of whole whose parts come one after another. Most famously, he showed that some of Abelard’s rules for conditionals seemed to force a contradiction. Alberic’s school also discussed thoughts, language, and how divine knowledge might relate to a changing future. Because the evidence is incomplete and often comes from anonymous manuscripts, scholars remain careful about which ideas should be assigned directly to Alberic.
key_ideas: Alberic was an important teacher and philosopher in twelfth-century Paris.
He strongly disagreed with Peter Abelard and his followers.
He thought logic was about real things as well as words.
He defended real universals, such as kinds and species.
He said that time can be a whole whose parts happen one after another.
He argued that Abelard’s rules for conditionals could lead to a contradiction.
summaries.why_it_matters: Alberic shows that philosophy is often built through disagreement. He asked whether words merely name things or whether logic reflects real features of the world. His debates also show why definitions and rules must be tested carefully: a rule that seems helpful may produce an impossible result when combined with other rules. Studying him gives us a window into medieval schools, where teachers used arguments to examine language, time, reality, and knowledge.

important_terms.definition: A thinker who studies big questions about reality, knowledge, language, and reasoning.
A statement or word used to describe something as belonging to a group or having a feature.
A general kind, such as animal, that can apply to more than one individual thing.
The study of what is real and what kinds of things exist.
Careful reasoning used to test whether an argument works.

questions_to_think_about: Is a group like “animals” only a word, or is there something real shared by animals?
Can something be a whole if some of its parts have already passed or have not happened yet?
Why might a philosopher test an opponent’s rules by building a strange argument?
How can studying old disagreements help us understand careful reasoning today?

summaries.example: Consider the conditional “If Socrates is human, then Socrates is an animal.” Abelard treated such a conditional as acceptable because being an animal is contained in being human. Alberic’s school could then examine a related conditional involving Socrates being human and not being an animal. Since Socrates is human and being human includes being an animal, the negative predication does not describe a genuine relation among things. For the Albricani, that failure helps explain why the argument does not establish the contradiction Abelard’s system appears to generate.
summaries.summary:
Alberic of Paris was one of the prominent philosophical teachers in twelfth-century Paris and the principal rival of Peter Abelard. His own works have not survived, so his philosophy must be reconstructed from references in medieval logical commentaries and texts associated with his school, the Albricani. This evidence is difficult to interpret because many manuscripts are anonymous, their dates are uncertain, and the attribution of some doctrines remains unsettled. The entry therefore distinguishes views explicitly attributed to Alberic from broader Albrican positions.

Alberic’s metaphysics is broadly realist in opposition to Abelardian antirealism. He held that logic concerns things as well as words, and that thing-predication is more fundamental than linguistic predication. A predicate is properly predicated of a subject only when the corresponding relation holds in reality; false combinations of terms do not express genuine predication. This account shapes his treatment of conditionals and allows his school to reject the premises of the so-called embarrassing arguments against Abelard.

Alberic also defended real universals. On the interpretation preserved in a commentary associated with his school, genera and species are present in sensible individuals and can be understood separately, but they do not exist independently of individuals. The theory is therefore not straightforward Platonism. It is also possible, on this view, for a universal to have only one instance: the phoenix was used as a stock example. The exact meaning of describing genera and species as “sorts of things,” and whether this theory belongs to Alberic himself, remains unclear.

key_ideas: Alberic’s philosophical context was the competitive school culture of twelfth-century Paris, where his main rival was Peter Abelard.
His metaphysics and logic are realist: the primary subject of logic is relations among things, not merely relations among linguistic expressions.
He distinguished several kinds of predication, with thing-predication as the fundamental kind.
The Albricani defended universals as things located in sensible individuals and allowed a universal to have only one actual instance, using the phoenix as an example.
Alberic treated time as a successive whole, whose past and future parts need not exist together for the whole to exist.
His criticism of Abelard’s theory of conditionals helped provoke new medieval approaches to consequence and logical validity.
summaries.why_it_matters: Alberic matters because he connects metaphysics and logic. His view that predication concerns things changes how one evaluates conditionals, negation, and contradiction. His dispute with Abelard also illustrates a major historical question: should logical consequence depend on truth alone, on relevant content, or on relations among real entities? The surviving evidence further teaches an important scholarly lesson. Historical philosophy often has to be reconstructed from incomplete, anonymous, and disputed sources, so responsible interpretation must separate firm attribution from plausible reconstruction.

important_terms.definition: The relation involved when a predicate is truly said of a subject; Alberic treated relation among things as more fundamental than relation among words.
A general entity or kind that is naturally suited to be predicated of many individuals.
A philosophical position holding that universals are real in individual things, without existing as separate Platonic objects.
An argument form in which a conclusion or rule exposes an apparently unacceptable result in an opponent’s theory.
A statement with an antecedent and a consequent, often expressed as “if...then.”
A whole whose parts exist successively rather than all at once, as with time, speech, or running.
The view that meaning or thought is determined by meaningful parts and how they are combined.
The position that God’s knowledge of future events changes as events occur, while this need not change the total amount of divine knowledge.

questions_to_think_about: Does saying that a universal is real in individuals explain what several individuals have in common, or merely rename the problem?
Should a theory of logical consequence concern truth, relevance, the structure of things, or some combination?
What is the difference between a whole whose parts coexist and a whole whose parts succeed one another?
Can an argument be valid within a theory yet reveal that the theory’s principles are jointly inconsistent?
Would changing knowledge necessarily imply a change in the knower?

summaries.example: Suppose your science club says, “Every phoenix is an animal.” A phoenix is a mythical bird usually described as having only one example at a time. Abelard’s followers might say that “animal” cannot be a universal if it applies to only one thing, because a universal should apply to many. Alberic’s school disagreed. They focused on what the word is naturally able to describe, not only on how many examples happen to exist. So they could call “animal” a universal even in the one-phoenix case.
summaries.summary:
Alberic of Paris taught during the lively and competitive intellectual culture of twelfth-century Paris. He was known especially for opposing Peter Abelard and the Nominalist school associated with him. We know surprisingly little about Alberic’s life. He taught by the 1130s, may have spent time in Italy, and remained influential through students and later teachers. No writing by him is known to survive, so historians reconstruct his thought from medieval manuscripts, many of which are anonymous or difficult to date. This makes some attributions uncertain.

The central philosophical disagreement was about realism. Alberic treated logic as connected to metaphysics, the study of what exists. Logic was not merely a game with words. It also concerned relations among things. For example, when we say that a human is an animal, Alberic’s followers thought the important relation was between the things human and animal, not only between the words “human” and “animal.” They called this thing-predication. False combinations of terms do not automatically describe real predication, and negative statements work by excluding a relation rather than adding a positive thing-to-thing relation.

Alberic’s school defended real universals. A universal is a general kind that can be predicated of many individuals. Their view was not simple Platonism: genera and species were located in sensible things and depended on individuals, although the mind could understand them separately from individual features. The school also argued that a universal could have one instance. The phoenix served as an example, since it was imagined as having one instance at a time. Scholars still debate exactly how the school’s “sorts of things” theory should be understood and whether it originated with Alberic himself
key_ideas: Twelfth-century Paris had competing teachers and schools, and Alberic became a major opponent of Abelard’s Nominalists.
Alberic’s followers said that logic concerns real things, not just names and sentences.
They treated universals as real kinds found in individual things, while rejecting the idea that universals exist in a separate world.
Alberic allowed a universal to have just one actual example, unlike Abelard’s school.
He explained time as a changing whole made from parts that occur successively.
His criticism of Abelard’s conditionals helped push medieval thinkers to develop new theories of logical consequence.
summaries.why_it_matters: Alberic’s work matters because it shows how disagreements about ordinary-looking statements can reveal deep assumptions. The question “What does ‘human’ mean?” becomes a question about whether general kinds are real. The question “If...then...” becomes a question about relevance, truth, and the structure of reality. His case also demonstrates how philosophy and history work together: we must examine arguments while also asking how securely the surviving evidence represents a thinker’s own position.

important_terms.definition: A general kind or feature that can be predicated of many individuals, such as animal or human.
The view that general kinds are real in individual things, rather than being only names.
Saying something about a subject, such as saying that a particular person is human.
A rule or statement of the form “if this, then that.”
A school or group formed around a teacher’s philosophical views.
A contradiction or troubling result produced by applying an argument or rule.

questions_to_think_about: If only one phoenix existed, would “animal” still name a universal? Why?
When we say “A tree is green,” are we mainly talking about words, thoughts, or the tree itself?
Why might time need different rules from a box whose parts are all present together?
What should we do when an argument follows accepted rules but ends in a contradiction?
Why is it important to distinguish Alberic’s own views from ideas held only by his followers?
